extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and reporters (news writers and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing which events or stories journalists and editors should cover, using established 'news values' models (Galtung & Ruge, 1973; Shoemaker et al., 1987). Explains individual criteria and how they influence editorial selection and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: How relevant is a news story to the audience in question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a California earthquake is almost always more relevant to a West Coast audience than to an audience in Calcutta. Evaluators should consider the intended audience when assessing a story's importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: How recently did the event unfold? Recent events, or events in the making, are most likely to lead the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is of the utmost importance in today’s 24-hour news cycle. Shoemaker et al. also recognize timeliness as a critical news value; stories that are current or developing gain priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story can be easily simplified or summarized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that can be easily simplified or summarized are likely to be featured more prominently than stories that are convoluted or difficult to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event occurs on a predictable schedule and thus gains attention as it approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include elections, major sporting events, astrological events, and legal decisions; as these events draw closer they typically gain news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event is unpredictable (sudden/unexpected occurrences gain news value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events like natural disasters, accidents, or crimes are completely unpredictable and are likely to have significant news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event requires ongoing coverage and thus stays in the news over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some events—such as war, elections, protests, and strikes—require continuing coverage and are likely to remain in the news for a long time, though not always as the lead story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: How a potential story fits into the outlet’s overall mix of content (the editorial 'big picture').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider the sum of all content; they might select soft human-interest stories to balance hard-hitting investigative pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite People (Prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving prominent individuals (politicians, entertainers, athletes) are more newsworthy by virtue of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone throws a shoe at an everyday person, it’s probably not news. If someone throws a shoe at the President of the United States, it will likely be in the news for weeks. Shoemaker et al. label this as 'Prominence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite Countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in wealthy, developed countries tend to attract more attention than similar events in developing countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famine, drought, and national disasters are more likely to draw attention if they occur in elite countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity (Conflict/Controversy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad news, conflict, or controversy is generally regarded as more newsworthy than good news or peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors generally deem conflict more newsworthy than peace; Shoemaker et al. list 'Conflict or Controversy' as a core value and note its similarity to Gatlung and Ruge’s 'Negativity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic or cultural closeness of an event to the intended audience increases its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to Galtung and Ruge’s 'Relevance.' Huge local or regional stories might not make national news because they lack proximity to a broader audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / Impact / Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: How many people the event will impact and the magnitude of its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues like climate change have become major news because they affect large populations or have far-reaching consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest (Human Interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the story appeals to basic human interests or emotions (e.g., inspirational personal stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the inspirational story of a person overcoming large odds appeals to human interest and gains news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a story is sensational or lurid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational stories tend to make the front pages more than the everyday; outlets may favor sensational elements that attract attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Oddity / Unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: How strange, novel, or unusual a story is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strange stories are likely to find their way into the news. Example phrasing from the page: 'Dog bites man—no story. Man bites dog—story.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate news values satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall number or combination of news values a story satisfies affects its likelihood of coverage and prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states: 'The more of these news values a story satisfies, the more likely you are to see it prominently featured in mass media outlets.' Editors assess multiple values together when selecting stories.
